findings.summary: THE NEW LEASE-RELEASE EXIT CALLS delegate.close() WITH THE COMMITTER'S INTERRUPT FLAG SET, so in one of the two death shapes this diff itself tests for, the lease is exactly as stuck as before the fix. drainLoop's InterruptedException branch re-arms the flag (BatchingSequencer.java:315) and then returns `stopping` as the death cause (line 325); drainForever therefore reaches closeDelegateQuietly() on a thread that carries an interrupt. `LocalSequencer.close` is `leases.release()`, which falls through to `BoundedLock.takeOrFail` when `tryLock()` loses (LeaseManager.release), and `takeOrFail` does `lock.tryLock(bound, NANOSECONDS)`, which throws InterruptedException IMMEDIATELY when the flag is already set (BoundedLock.java:52-58); it then wraps it as IOException, `catch (Exception releaseFailed)` swallows it, and line 285-287 logs 'it will now survive to its TTL'. Any NIO/S3-backed store also raises ClosedByInterruptException on the PUT inside releaseLocked for the same reason -- the class's own comment at line 309-312 names that idiom as the realistic one. This is the SAME hazard the same commit documents at length for close() and fixes there with `boolean wasInterrupted = Thread.interrupted();` (line 421); the new path omits it. The one-line remedy is to clear the flag before `delegate.close()` in closeDelegateQuietly (no restore needed -- the committer is terminating).
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED in a copy of the staged tree (probe deleted afterwards). Delegate whose commitAll uses the textbook idiom `Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new IOException("the store call was interrupted")` -- the exact shape BatchingSequencer.java:309-312 says BoundedLock already uses -- and whose close() models BoundedLock.takeOrFail under contention by throwing IOException when the calling thread is interrupted. Result printed by the probe: `closeSawInterrupt=true leaseReleased=false`. So the ERROR line at 244-247 announces 'its lease is being released so another node can take over' and the lease is NOT released: the pod holds a lease it can no longer commit through until the TTL expires, which is precisely the TTL-bound failover the new block, its javadoc, and BatchingSequencerTerminationTest's class comment all say it exists to avoid. The diff's own test for this shape, aDelegateThatRESTORESTheInterruptFlagDoesNotStrandEveryLaterCaller, cannot see it because its delegate close is `closed.set(true)` -- interrupt-INSENSITIVE, verbatim the fixture weakness round 6 named and closed for close() in this same commit.

findings.summary: UNBOUNDED DELEGATE I/O WAS INSERTED BETWEEN THE DOOR SHUTTING AND THE QUEUE BEING FAILED, inverting the order close() uses and documents. In drainForever's finally the sequence is now `stop(); ... closeDelegateQuietly(); failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure());`. close() does the opposite -- `failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure())` at line 440 and only then `delegate.close()` at 447 -- with the comment at 438-439 saying why ('so anything the committer put back cannot be stranded'), and it additionally bounds its wait with `committer.join(Duration.ofSeconds(10))`. The committer's exit path has neither protection: `LeaseManager.release` can block up to the full TTL in `BoundedLock.takeOrFail` and then issue a store PUT that nothing in this codebase bounds, and every caller already queued sits on `PendingCommit.await` -> `CompletableFuture.join`, which the class's own comments repeatedly note is UNINTERRUPTIBLE. Worse, `closeDelegateQuietly` catches only `Exception`: an Error out of `delegate.close()` escapes the finally and `failAll(drainRemaining(), ...)` never runs at all, which contradicts the invariant stated at line 216-217 ('SO THE LOOP BODY CANNOT EXIT WITH THE DOOR OPEN. Every exit runs the finally, which shuts it and fails whatever is queued'). Remedy: fail the queue first, then close the delegate -- same order as close().
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED in a copy of the staged tree, twice (probes deleted afterwards). Caller 1 is inside a delegate commitAll that parks, then throws OutOfMemoryError; caller 2 enqueues after the batch was already drained, so it can only be failed by drainRemaining() in the exit path. (a) With a delegate whose close() blocks on a latch -- modelling a slow lease release -- caller 2 was still parked 3 s after the exit path had entered delegate.close(), printed as `queued caller still parked while delegate.close() is in flight = true`, and only completed when the close was released. (b) With `close()` throwing `new StackOverflowError(...)`, caller 2 was still parked after 5 s and never completes: the Error escapes `catch (Exception)`, aborts the finally before failAll, and leaves the caller on an uninterruptible join -- a producer thread hung until SIGKILL, which is the exact failure BatchingSequencerLifecycleTest's class comment says every test in it exists to prevent. Before this round the same finally was `stop(); failAll(...)` with nothing between them, so this is new surface introduced by the round-6 fix.

findings.summary: The comment claims 'Unlike the committer's exit this one still PROPAGATES: close is declared throws IOException and a caller shutting a pod down needs to hear that the lease did not come back.' In the case the CAS exists for -- committer died first, closeDelegateQuietly ran, delegate.close() failed and was swallowed at line 284-288 -- claimDelegateClose() returns false, close() skips the delegate entirely and returns cleanly, so the caller does NOT hear that the lease did not come back. The operator still gets the ERROR log, so this is a truthfulness gap in the comment rather than a lost signal.
findings.failure_scenario: A pod shuts down after its committer already died and its quiet lease release failed. `batching.close()` returns normally; the shutdown sequence proceeds as though the lease were handed back, when it will in fact survive to its TTL. Recorded, not blocking: per review.md, fixing a minor is permitted and usually wrong.
